#4426. Scientists finally discover how a common gut bacterium can trigger colon cancer

For nearly two decades, scientists have known that a common gut bacterium can produce a toxin that damages the colon and helps drive the formation of tumors. What they could not explain was how the toxin first attaches to intestinal cells and begins its attack. Now, researchers have uncovered that missing step, revealing a surprising vulnerability that could lead to new ways of protecting the colon.

The breakthrough comes from a team led by scientists at the Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center, its Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, and the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine. Their findings, published in Nature, identify a protein called claudin-4 as the essential docking point for a bacterial toxin known as BFT.

Even more promising, the researchers have already used this discovery to develop a molecular decoy that intercepts the toxin before it can damage colon cells. The strategy successfully protected mice from the toxin's harmful effects, suggesting a possible new approach to preventing bacterial damage associated with colorectal cancer. The research received partial support from the National Institutes of Health.

"We've made several attempts over time to identify the receptor, so this is an exciting moment," says senior author Cynthia Sears, M.D., Bloomberg~Kimmel Professor of Cancer Immunotherapy and professor of medicine at Johns Hopkins. "Understanding how bacterial toxins work can open doors to new approaches for detection and therapy for associated diseases, including diarrhea, colorectal cancer and bloodstream infections."

How a Common Gut Bacterium Can Promote Colon Cancer

The investigation centers on Bacteroides fragilis, a bacterium that can be found in the intestines of up to 20% of healthy people. Although the presence of this bacterium does not automatically mean someone will develop cancer, certain strains produce a powerful toxin capable of disrupting the colon's protective lining, causing inflammation, and encouraging tumor growth.

The toxin, known as B. fragilis toxin or BFT, has been under investigation for years. In a landmark 2009 study published in Nature Medicine, Sears and her colleagues demonstrated that the toxin could promote the development of colon tumors. Their work helped establish an important connection between toxin-producing gut bacteria, chronic inflammation, and colorectal cancer.

Earlier experiments also revealed that BFT damages a protein called E-cadherin, which helps hold neighboring cells together and maintain the colon's protective barrier. When this protein is broken apart, the barrier becomes compromised, potentially allowing harmful substances and bacteria to interfere with the surrounding tissue.

However, one critical question remained unanswered. Although BFT could break down E-cadherin, the toxin did not appear to attach directly to that protein. Researchers suspected that another molecule was helping the toxin reach its target, but repeated attempts to identify it had failed.

Scientists Identify the Missing Link Using CRISPR

To solve the mystery, the researchers turned to CRISPR, a powerful gene-editing technology that allows scientists to selectively disable genes and investigate what they do.

Maxwell White, an M.D./Ph.D. candidate working in Sears' laboratory, led a genome-wide CRISPR screening effort in collaboration with Matthew Waldor's laboratory at Harvard Medical School. The team systematically switched off genes in colon epithelial cells, the cells that form the inner lining of the colon, to determine which ones were necessary for the toxin to attach and cause damage.

One gene stood out dramatically. It produces claudin-4, a protein that helps neighboring cells form tight junctions, the seals that limit the movement of substances between cells and help maintain the intestinal barrier.

When the researchers disabled the gene responsible for claudin-4, BFT could no longer bind to the colon cells. Without that initial attachment, the toxin was unable to attack E-cadherin.

The finding revealed that claudin-4 acts as a receptor for the bacterial toxin. In effect, the toxin must first latch onto this protein before it can carry out its damaging activity.

"It took a while to get the assay working and validate the approach, but once we were able to do the screen, claudin-4 was a clear, resounding top hit," says White. "That was an exciting moment."

An Unexpected Discovery Reveals a New Bacterial Attack Strategy

The identity of the receptor surprised the scientists.

Sears and other researchers had expected BFT to interact with a protein involved in cellular signaling, such as a G protein-coupled receptor. These receptors act somewhat like communication switches, allowing cells to respond to signals from their surroundings.

Claudin-4, however, serves a very different purpose. Rather than functioning primarily as a signaling receptor, it helps maintain the physical connections between neighboring cells.

The discovery also revealed an unusual way for a bacterial toxin to operate. BFT belongs to a class of enzymes called proteases, which cut other proteins. Most proteases act directly on their targets, but BFT appears to require a separate receptor before it can reach and damage E-cadherin.

When the team reviewed previous scientific research, they could not identify another toxin known to use the same mechanism.

To establish that BFT and claudin-4 truly bind to each other, the Johns Hopkins researchers collaborated with structural biologists F. Xavier Gomis-Rüth and Ulrich Eckhard at the Molecular Biology Institute of Barcelona.

Using techniques that measure how molecules interact, White and the Barcelona team showed that BFT and claudin-4 form a tightly bound complex in laboratory experiments. Each toxin molecule paired with one receptor molecule, providing direct physical evidence of the connection.

A Clever Molecular Decoy Blocks the Dangerous Gut Toxin

Identifying the receptor did more than explain how the toxin works. It also gave the scientists an idea for stopping it.

If BFT needs claudin-4 to attach to colon cells, perhaps a substitute could lure the toxin away from its intended target.

To test that possibility, the team developed a molecular decoy. This was a soluble protein carrying sequences from claudin-4, designed to attract BFT without allowing it to attack the colon's protective lining.

The researchers then worked with Min Dong's laboratory at Harvard Medical School, including Kang Wang and colleagues, to investigate the approach in mice. These experiments allowed the scientists to examine how the toxin behaves in the more complicated environment of a living intestine.

The results were encouraging. Instead of binding to claudin-4 receptors on colon cells, BFT attached to the decoy proteins. By intercepting the toxin, the decoys successfully protected the mice from BFT-induced damage.

The finding suggests that it may be possible to interfere with the toxin's first step rather than trying to repair the damage after it occurs.

"This approach could be iterated upon with small molecules or other biologics that have better pharmacological properties," says White. The team is now exploring which molecular approaches might be most successful to block the toxin.

Small molecules are compounds that can sometimes be developed into medicines, while biologics are treatments made from or involving biological materials, such as proteins. Future versions of the decoy strategy could potentially be designed to work more effectively in the body or be easier to administer.

What This Discovery Could Mean for Colon Cancer Prevention

Although the findings identify a promising new target, important questions remain.

Scientists have established that BFT attaches to claudin-4 and that blocking this interaction can protect mice from toxin-induced damage. However, they have not yet captured the exact experimental three-dimensional structure showing how the two molecules fit together.

Even advanced artificial intelligence tools, including AlphaFold, have been unable to fully resolve the interaction. Understanding its precise structure could help researchers design more effective compounds that prevent the toxin from binding.

Further experiments will also be needed to determine whether the decoy approach can safely and effectively prevent toxin-related disease in humans. The mouse experiments demonstrated protection against tissue damage, but they did not establish that the strategy prevents colorectal cancer.

Nevertheless, the discovery resolves a major question that has persisted since the connection between BFT and colon tumor formation was established in 2009. By identifying the toxin's previously unknown point of attachment, researchers have uncovered a potential way to interrupt a harmful biological process before it begins.

The findings could ultimately support new strategies for detecting or treating conditions associated with bacterial toxins, including colorectal cancer, diarrhea, and bloodstream infections.

Additional researchers who contributed to the study include Jason Chen, Shaoguang Wu, Abby L. Geis, and Jessica Queen of Johns Hopkins, along with Hailong Zhang, Karthik Hullahalli, and Jie Zhang of Harvard Medical School.

Funding was provided by the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, Janssen Research and Development, Cancer Research UK, the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R01 AI042347, R01 NS080833, R01 NS117626, R01 AI170835 and R01 AI189789) and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute.

#4424. Team Liquid sweep Anyone’s Legend out of Worlds 2026, ending NA’s 13-series LPL drought

Team Liquid Alienware beat Anyone's Legend 2-0 to eliminate the LPL's top seed from the Worlds 2026 Swiss Stage without a game win. The result keeps the LCS champions alive and sets up a deciding series against LOS on 30 October.

Anyone’s Legend arrived at Worlds 2026 as China’s top seed. Team Liquid Alienware delivered the final blow in a series that began at 15:55 CDT.

Liquid controlled the opening game from the red side. They closed it in 33 minutes and 13 seconds with a 16-5 lead on kills. Top laner Morgan finished 7/1/6 on Camille. The second game was a far longer contest. It ran to 47 minutes before Liquid sealed the series, with Yeon’s Xayah playing a key part in the result.

For Anyone’s Legend, the defeat capped a collapse. They had already lost best-of-one matches to Karmine Corp and Top Esports before the Liquid series. Such an exit had no precedent for a Chinese top seed at Worlds, Dot Esports reported. It is also the second Worlds in a row in which the LPL’s first seed failed to get out of the Swiss Stage. Bilibili Gaming went out in Round 5 in 2025.

Anyone’s Legend and Team Secret Whales were the first two teams knocked out. Each finished joint 15th-16th and receives US$90,000 from a total prize pool of US$5,000,000. Earlier the same day, LOS had eliminated Team Secret Whales, the LCP’s top seed, with a 2-0 win that gave Brazil its first victory of the Swiss Stage.

The significance stretches beyond this tournament. Fittingly, the LCS’s previous series win over an LPL team also belonged to Team Liquid. They beat Invictus Gaming in the MSI 2019 semi-finals.

Liquid came into Worlds as the LCS’s first seed. They earned that spot by beating LYON 3-1 in the 2026 Summer grand final on 4 October. Their Swiss Stage campaign started badly, however. Defeats to CTBC Flying Oyster and Bilibili Gaming left them a loss away from elimination before the Anyone’s Legend series.

The sweep leaves Liquid ninth on a 1-2 series record and 2-2 on games. Under the Swiss format, teams go through to the Knockout Stage with three match wins and are knocked out with three losses. Elimination and advancement matches are played as best-of-three with Fearless Draft.

#4422. New diabetes implant uses electricity to lower blood sugar and promote weight loss

An experimental electronic implant could offer an entirely new way to treat type 2 diabetes. Rather than relying on insulin or conventional medications, the device uses electricity to convert excess blood sugar into a substance that the body can eliminate. In early tests with diabetic mice, the technology successfully regulated blood sugar and also led to weight loss.

The development comes as type 2 diabetes continues to affect a growing number of people worldwide. Unlike type 1 diabetes, type 2 is frequently associated with obesity, limited physical activity, and consuming more energy than the body needs over long periods.

Insulin injections can help reduce blood sugar by allowing muscle cells to absorb glucose from the bloodstream. However, insulin does not eliminate the underlying problem of excess energy. When the body does not use the glucose it absorbs, the surplus can eventually be converted into fat. This helps explain why some people with diabetes continue gaining weight even while receiving treatment.

Researchers led by Martin Fussenegger, a professor in the Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering at ETH Zurich in Basel, have developed an implant designed to address this problem differently. Their findings were published in the journal Science.

A New Diabetes Treatment Powered by Electricity

Fussenegger and his colleagues have spent years developing technologies capable of controlling blood sugar. Their previous designs used engineered genetic networks, but these systems depended on living cells and other biological materials.

That dependence introduced several complications. Biological components can create challenges involving immune compatibility, long-term stability, production, and regulatory approval.

The researchers have now taken a different approach by creating a catalyst made entirely from inorganic materials. It performs its function without requiring living cells, enzymes, or other biological components.

At the heart of the implant is a piece of graphite felt covered with tiny clusters of gold. These gold structures are coated with even smaller platinum particles, creating a specially engineered surface that enables the chemical reaction needed to process glucose.

The researchers designed this nanoscale surface themselves. According to Fussenegger, the materials also demonstrated excellent biocompatibility during experimental testing, suggesting they can interact with living tissue without causing significant adverse reactions.

The system includes an electronic controller enclosed in a 3D-printed housing. Instead of relying on a conventional wired power connection, the implant receives energy wirelessly at a frequency of 13.56 MHz. This frequency is internationally allocated for industrial, scientific, and medical applications.

How the Implant Removes Excess Blood Sugar

The technology works by transforming excess glucose into gluconate, a substance that can be eliminated from the body through urine.

Normally, glucose provides energy for cells. When more glucose is available than the body needs, some of that excess energy can ultimately be stored as fat. By converting part of the glucose into gluconate, the implant prevents that portion from being metabolized and stored in tissues, potentially helping reduce fat accumulation.

The entire process is designed to happen automatically, responding to changes in blood sugar as they occur.

A conventional glucose sensor, similar to those worn on the upper arm by many people with diabetes, continuously measures glucose concentrations in tissue. When levels rise too high, such as after a meal, the sensor communicates through Bluetooth with a smartphone or smartwatch.

The connected device then activates the implant, supplying the electrical energy needed for the catalyst to convert glucose into gluconate.

Once glucose levels return to the desired range, the implant automatically shuts down. This feedback system, known as closed-loop control, is intended to prevent blood sugar from dropping dangerously low.

Blood Sugar Control and Weight Loss in Diabetic Mice

To evaluate the technology, the researchers first conducted a laboratory experiment using a reservoir containing 5 liters of a nutrient solution with glucose. That volume is approximately equal to the amount of blood circulating in an adult human body.

The experiment demonstrated that the catalyst could convert glucose in a solution of this scale, an important step toward assessing its potential for medical applications.

The researchers then implanted the system in diabetic mice. The results showed that the device could precisely regulate the animals' blood sugar levels. The mice also lost weight, suggesting that converting excess glucose rather than allowing it to contribute to fat storage could offer an additional metabolic benefit.

Over six weeks of testing, the implant continued functioning reliably and was well tolerated by the animals.

"The system operates at a very low voltage, and our experiments showed no evidence of tissue damage from either electrical or thermal effects," says Fussenegger.

Although these findings are promising, the device has not yet been tested in humans. Additional research will be necessary to determine whether the technology can operate safely and effectively in people with diabetes.

Could Electronics Transform the Future of Diabetes Treatment?

Fussenegger believes the technology could represent a fundamental change in how diabetes is managed. Rather than using medications to influence how the body processes glucose, an electronic device could directly control the amount of glucose available.

"For decades, we have treated diabetes by telling the body how to manage glucose. We are now showing that we can take control of glucose directly, using electronics rather than drugs," he says. "And the catalyst only activates when glucose levels are too high."

The approach also creates opportunities to connect medical treatments with digital technologies, including the Internet of Things. This refers to networks of devices that exchange information and respond automatically to changing conditions.

The researchers envision electronically controlled treatments that could be manufactured at scale and integrated with existing digital health systems.

Their next objective is to turn the experimental implant into a medical device suitable for further development and eventual clinical testing.

One potential advantage is its relatively simple glucose conversion mechanism. Because the catalyst does not rely on cells or enzymes, the researchers believe some of the technical challenges associated with biological treatments could be easier to overcome.

Much of the supporting technology is also already available. Wireless power transmission systems and external electronic controllers are commercially established, meaning the team would not need to develop every component from scratch.

If future studies demonstrate similar benefits in humans, this approach could open the door to a new class of diabetes treatments in which smart electronic devices help regulate blood sugar directly, potentially reducing reliance on conventional medications.

#4421. Genesis GV60 Magma Doesn’t Sacrifice Speed for Faux-Shift Fun

Unlike its Ioniq 5 N fraternal twin, the electric Genesis GV60 Magma is just as quick simulating shifts as in its standard drive mode.

Welcome to Car and Driver's Testing Hub, where we zoom in on the test numbers. We've been pushing vehicles to their limits since 1956 to provide objective data to bolster our subjective impressions (you can see how we test here).

When the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N arrived on the scene back in 2023, it introduced simulated shifting to electric vehicles. We were so enthralled by its combustion-engine cosplay that it played a major part in the 5 N being named our 2024 EV of the Year. As fun as it is to bang through gears in a vehicle without an engine, our testing proved that the 5 N’s acceleration times significantly suffered in “N e-Shift” mode compared with its standard drive mode. Like the Ioniq 5 N, the new Genesis GV60 Magma—the luxury brand’s first entry in its performance-focused Magma sub-brand—features a “Virtual Gear Shift” mode that mimics the sensations of an eight-speed dual-clutch automatic paired to an internal-combustion engine. But this time, it doesn’t come at a performance cost.

See all results for new 2027 Genesis GV60 Magma for sale near 29405

Beneath the surface, the Ioniq 5 N and the GV60 Magma feature nearly identical hardware. Both are built on Hyundai Motor Group's E-GMP electric vehicle platform, feature a dual-motor all-wheel drive powertrain that produces up to 641 horsepower, make use of an 84-kWh battery pack, and both roll on 275/35R-21 Pirelli P Zero Elect tires, although the Magma gets newer PZ5-spec rubber versus the Ioniq 5 N’s PZ4 Pirellis. Besides the GV60 Magma’s nearly four-inch-shorter wheelbase and 91-pound-heavier curb weight, the differences between the pair are primarily software-related or matters of styling and design.

Some of those discrepancies are superficial—the 5 N’s faux-engine soundtrack mimics a 7750-rpm inline-four while the Magma’s aural signature is based on a 9000-rpm V-6, for example—but others have an impact on performance. Both models can only access their max power output with a time-limited Boost mode, and while the Hyundai can maintain its 641-hp peak in 10-second bursts, the Genesis can continue at full tilt in 15-second increments. That longer duration of peak output allows the Magma to walk away from the 5 N as they approach their Vmax—for example, the Genesis beats the Hyundai to 150 mph by almost two seconds—but otherwise the two were bumper-to-bumper up to 120 mph. The real delta between the Hyundai and Genesis’s straight-line capabilities only surfaces once both are switched into their simulated-shift drive modes.

See all results for new 2027 Genesis GV60 Magma for sale near 29405

The last time we had an Ioniq 5 N at our test track, we performed two separate acceleration runs, once without N e-Shift and once with it activated. Importantly, N e-Shift mode disables the 5 N’s N Grin Boost and launch-control features, essentially robbing it of 40 horsepower and an optimized start, so we conducted the first run without launch control to even the playing field a bit. Still, the 5 N proved to be significantly quicker when it wasn’t hammering through make-believe gears, silently rocketing to 60 mph in 3.1 seconds, reaching 100 mph in 7.2 seconds, and crossing the quarter-mile marker in 11.3 seconds. With N e-Shift activated, it took the Ioniq 5 N 3.5 seconds to reach 60 mph (a four-tenth increase), 8.3 seconds to hit 100 mph (a whopping 1.1 seconds slower than in its standard drive mode), and 11.8 seconds to clear the quarter-mile (five-tenths behind our non-N e-Shift run).

When we conducted the same experiment in the GV60 Magma, we got very different results. During our testing, the Magma achieved nearly identical acceleration figures regardless of its drive mode. In both of its runs, the Genesis managed a 3.0-second sprint to 60 mph, a 6.8-second dash to 100 mph, and a quarter-mile time of 11.0 seconds. (The 0.1-second difference between our reported quarter-mile time of 11.1 seconds for the Magma and the 11.0-second figure quoted here is that, in this case, we were comparing two runs in the same direction, while all of our official acceleration figures are an average of a run in each direction.)

Given that the 5 N and Magma feature nearly identical specs and that all other environmental factors were equal, what gives? To us, the answer seems pretty straightforward. Unlike in the 5 N, engaging the Magma’s Virtual Gear Shift mode doesn’t lock out its boost or launch-control functions, allowing it to access its full 641-hp output and a “6000-rpm,” traction-aided takeoff whether it is fake shifting or not. The additional 40 horsepower and better getaway also explain why the Genesis’s fake-shift acceleration figures are far better than the Hyundai’s, with the Magma beating the 5 N to 60 mph by 0.5 second, to 100 mph by 1.5 seconds, and to the quarter-mile by 0.8 second. Ultimately, the Ioniq 5 N forces you to choose between its primary party trick and peak performance, while the GV60 Magma lets you have your cake and eat it too.

Genesis’s smallest SUV is the electric GV60, which is offered in a variety of flavors from the tame rear-wheel drive base model to the wild, 641-hp Magma performance trim. While the standard model is set up primarily for comfort, the GV60 Magma adds plenty of aggression to the formula.

Driving range for the base rear-wheel-drive model is highest in the bunch at 306 miles per charge. Going with all-wheel drive or the Magma trim reduces driving range dramatically, but all models offer quick charging times thanks to a robust 800-volt architecture.

Expert Tip: Genesis makes it clear that the ultimate goal of the GV60 Magma is to offer a sophisticated take on performance, melded with plenty of luxury rather than rip-your-guts-out performance; if EV ferocity is your sole desire, check out the Ioniq 5 N.

Compare the 2027 Genesis GV60 with the top vehicles in this segment with our new compare tool.

The GV60 Magma is a new variant this year, spearheading the GV60’s push into the performance EV class. It replaces last year’s Performance trim. 2027 also sees the introduction of an all-wheel-drive Prestige trim that bridges the gap between the base GV60 model and the new Magma.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

The rear-wheel-drive GV60 Standard gets motivation from a single rear-mounted 225-hp motor; going with all-wheel drive adds a front motor for a combined 314 horsepower. The GV60 Magma boosts output to 641 ponies.

The GV60's road manners are quite refined. When cruising, the cabin remains whisper quiet; encounter a stretch of winding road, though, and the GV60 offers enough athleticism to entertain the driver and enough surefootedness to inspire confidence. The chassis has been recalibrated for the Magma with specific damper and power distribution metrics, along with chunky 275/35R-21 tires specially developed for the Magma by Pirelli.

In addition to Launch Control and Boost mode, drivers have a choice of three additional drive modes: Sprint, GT, and MY, the latter allowing for customization of the electronically controlled limited-slip differential, stability control, and other performance factors. There's also a drift mode, but Genesis is careful not to call it a "drive" mode for normal street use. When we drove the GV60 Magma, we found it to be nimble in the corners and more polished than the Ioniq 5 N.

In Comparison: The Ioniq 5 N, with an identical 641 horsepower in Boost mode, also ripped to 60 mph in 3.0 seconds in our testing.

Although most buyers likely won't hook a trailer up to the GV60, it can tow up to 2000 pounds.

The GV60 uses a lithium-ion battery with 84 kW of usable capacity. The rear-wheel-drive base model offers the most range at 306 miles per charge, while the Magma trim offers the least at 220 miles. In our real-world 75-mph highway range test, the Magma went just 200 miles. DC fast charging is available, with Genesis claiming the GV60 can be replenished from 10-to-80 percent in just 18 minutes. C/D testing corroborates this claim, as our test vehicle replenished the battery from 13 percent to 80 percent in 18 minutes. Genesis says a level 2 AC charger can replenish the battery from 10 to 100 percent in about seven hours.

The EPA estimates that the rear-wheel drive GV60 should deliver up to 119 MPGe city, 101 MPGe highway, and 110 MPGe combined. All-wheel-drive models are rated for up to 107 MPGe city, 93 MPGe highway, and 100 MPGe combined. The Magma is rated for 84 MPGe city, 72 MPGe highway, and 78 MPGe combined. MPGe stands for miles per gallon of gas equivalent, an EPA metric that estimates PHEV and EV fuel efficiency. For more information about the GV60's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

First Row: Though the Genesis GV60 isn't as spacious as its larger GV70 and GV80 siblings, it offers a slightly more modern interior that embraces the high-tech concept. Whereas the GV70 and GV80 take a more traditional luxury approach, the GV60 integrates some cool motifs and features, including a center-console gear selector that flips upside down when in park and has the appearance of a crystal ball. The Magma model gets a unique look all its own, with the seats, doors, and the center console sporting synthetic suede upholstery highlighted with Magma Orange and grey stitching. A Magma-exclusive steering wheel features orange accents on the control buttons.

Second Row: Rear seat space and comfort are expected to be the same as the non-Magma GV60, but we wouldn’t rule out more aggressive bolstering that might make fitting three across difficult or impossible.

Cargo Capacity: Behind the GV60 Magma's rear seat is a 24.0-cubic-foot cargo bay. With the rear seats folded, that cargo volume grows to 54.7 cubic feet. A tiny frunk offering just 0.71 cubes of storage resides under the SUV's hood. With all the seats up, the standard GV60 accommodated seven carry-on bags in C/D testing.

A large 27.0-inch touchscreen display stretches across the GV60 Magma's dashboard. It provides room for a digital gauge cluster as well as a central infotainment screen. Bluetooth, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, in-dash navigation, a head-up display, and a wireless smartphone charging pad are all standard. An eight-speaker stereo is standard; a premium Bang & Olufsen setup with 17 speakers is optional.

All GV60 Magma models come fully loaded with Genesis's driver-assistance features, including parking sensors, blind-spot monitoring, lane-keeping assist, and a lane-centering feature.

For information about the GV60’s crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

The Genesis warranty coverage exceeds the typical term limits for the luxury segment. The GV60 comes with powertrain coverage for up to 10 years or 100,000 miles and complimentary scheduled maintenance for three years or 36,000 miles.

#4419. Scientists find surprisingly little evidence that medical cannabis helps you sleep

A major new scientific review is raising questions about whether medical cannabis actually helps people with insomnia. Despite growing interest in cannabis as a sleep treatment, researchers found that the available evidence is too weak to reliably determine whether it improves sleep quality, sleep duration, or how well people function during the day.

Insomnia affects millions of people and can make it difficult to fall asleep, remain asleep throughout the night, or wake up feeling rested. Beyond the frustration of sleepless nights, the condition can seriously disrupt daily life and increase the likelihood of developing anxiety or depression.

Treatments for insomnia include cognitive behavioral therapy, which helps people change thoughts and habits that interfere with sleep, as well as medications such as antidepressants and antipsychotics. However, these approaches do not work equally well for everyone, fueling interest in alternative options.

Medical cannabis has attracted particular attention because of its potential to improve sleep. Unlike recreational cannabis, regulated medical products typically contain carefully measured amounts of THC and CBD, two compounds found in cannabis, and are administered as tablets, sprays, or oils. Despite its growing popularity, scientists have continued to debate whether cannabis offers meaningful benefits for people with insomnia.

Major Review Finds Little Evidence of Sleep Benefits

To investigate, researchers from The Cochrane Associate Centre at the Universidad Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires and the University of Manitoba examined nine clinical studies involving 537 adults between the ages of 18 and 76 who were receiving treatment for insomnia.

Most of the studies involved people with primary insomnia, meaning their sleep problems were not attributed to another medical condition. Eight trials compared regulated medical cannabis with a placebo, an inactive treatment used to measure whether a therapy produces genuine benefits. The remaining trial compared cannabis with amitriptyline, an antidepressant that is sometimes used to treat sleep problems.

Across the placebo comparisons, medical cannabis produced little or no clinically meaningful improvement in sleep quality, satisfaction with sleep, total hours slept, or daytime functioning.

The researchers also identified potential drawbacks. Participants who received medical cannabis were substantially more likely to experience mild side effects, including dizziness and dry mouth, than those given a placebo. However, this finding came from a relatively small number of studies, limiting confidence in the result.

There was some indication that medical cannabis might improve overall quality of life. Yet the evidence supporting this possibility was highly uncertain. When the findings were combined, the results were consistent with outcomes ranging from a slight decline in quality of life to a substantial improvement.

"The main message is that the research currently available is not sufficient to reliably answer whether medical cannabis helps people with insomnia," says Dr. Lucia Varela, lead author of the study from the University of Manitoba, Canada. "This does not mean that medical cannabis is ineffective. It means that, based on the evidence we have, we cannot draw reliable conclusions about its effectiveness for insomnia in the general population."

Why Scientists Remain Uncertain About Cannabis and Insomnia

One of the biggest problems was the quality of the research itself. The reviewers rated their confidence in the available evidence as low or very low, citing small study populations, conflicting findings, and potential bias in how the trials were conducted.

Another challenge was the lack of consistency between studies. Researchers tested different medical cannabis products, making it difficult to directly compare their results or determine whether particular formulations might work better than others.

The studies were also relatively short. The longest followed participants for just 12 weeks, leaving major unanswered questions about whether medical cannabis could provide lasting sleep benefits or produce additional effects with prolonged use.

More Research Is Needed Before Cannabis Can Be Recommended

The researchers also cautioned that the study participants did not adequately represent the broader population of people living with insomnia.

Women accounted for nearly three-quarters (72.66% of participants), and the research was heavily weighted toward younger adults. As a result, it remains unclear whether the findings would apply equally to men, older individuals, or people whose insomnia occurs alongside other medical conditions.

Taken together, these limitations mean that the existing research cannot establish whether medical cannabis is an effective insomnia treatment. The authors emphasize that larger, more rigorous clinical trials are needed before it can be confidently recommended for improving sleep.

Importantly, the findings do not establish that medical cannabis is ineffective. Instead, they highlight how much remains unknown about a treatment that has gained considerable attention despite limited high-quality evidence.

"The evidence is too weak and uncertain to draw firm conclusions about the use of medical cannabis for insomnia," says Dr. Luis Garegnani, senior author from Universidad Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires, Argentina. "Rather than viewing the findings as either an endorsement or a rejection of medical cannabis, clinicians and patients should recognize the uncertainty and consider individual circumstances while better evidence is generated."

Materials provided by Cochrane. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4417. Even moderate drinking linked to cancer and early death, major study finds

A major new study suggests that even modest amounts of alcohol may carry serious health consequences. Researchers found that drinking levels many Americans consider moderate are associated with higher risks of premature death, disability, cancer, heart disease, and other long-term health problems.

Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research challenges the longstanding belief that moderate drinking is harmless or may even provide health benefits. The findings suggest that alcohol's risks begin at relatively low levels of consumption and increase as people drink more.

"This study provides the most comprehensive U.S. estimates to date of lifetime risks of alcohol-attributable mortality and morbidity, showing that even moderate levels of consumption increase the risk of premature death and disability," said study co-author Katherine M. Keyes, PhD, professor of Epidemiology at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.

"No protective effect of drinking was observed even at low levels," added Keyes, whose research examines alcohol and other substance use across different stages of life.

"Even low levels of alcohol use come with health risks," said lead study author Kevin Shield, PhD, an associate professor at the University of Toronto and a senior scientist who leads the World Health Organization (WHO)/Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Collaborating Centre in Addiction and Mental Health. "And that risk continues to increase the more someone drinks."

Major Study Examines the Lifetime Health Risks of Alcohol

To better understand how drinking affects health over a lifetime, researchers from the United States and Canada conducted an extensive review of existing scientific evidence.

Medical experts evaluated more than 7,200 scientific articles examining diseases and injuries associated with alcohol consumption. They used this evidence to determine how drinking influences the risk of individual health conditions, then combined those findings with large national health data sets.

Using statistical models, the team estimated how different levels of alcohol consumption affect the likelihood of developing serious illnesses or dying prematurely over a lifetime.

The analysis covered a wide range of health problems linked to alcohol, including cardiovascular disease, liver disease, injuries, and several forms of cancer. Among the cancers examined were those affecting the esophagus, mouth, and breast.

By considering these conditions together, the researchers were able to estimate alcohol's overall health burden rather than focusing on individual diseases.

Why Two Drinks a Day May Be Riskier Than You Think

One of the study's most important findings concerns drinking habits that many people would not consider excessive.

Consuming two alcoholic drinks per day, a level often viewed as socially moderate, was associated with a substantially higher risk of premature death attributable to alcohol.

The findings also provide more specific information than the latest U.S. Dietary Guidelines, which recommend that Americans "limit alcoholic beverages" but do not identify a particular amount that can be consumed safely.

Earlier dietary recommendations set daily limits of two alcoholic drinks for men and one for women. However, what counts as a single drink depends on the beverage and its alcohol content. A standard drink generally corresponds to 12 ounces of beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of spirits, although differences in alcohol concentration can change those amounts.

According to the researchers, the newer guidelines communicate a useful 'less-is-best' principle but lack specific numerical estimates that would help people understand how health risks change with consumption.

Their analysis was intended to fill that gap by measuring risks across a broad range of drinking levels.

Does Moderate Drinking Have Any Health Benefits?

For years, moderate alcohol consumption has sometimes been promoted as beneficial for cardiovascular health. The new findings cast doubt on that idea when the full range of alcohol-related health effects is considered.

The researchers found no statistically significant protective effect on overall health at any level of alcohol consumption.

They acknowledged that relatively low alcohol intake may be associated with a reduced risk of ischemic heart disease and stroke. Ischemic heart disease occurs when reduced blood flow deprives the heart muscle of the oxygen it needs, often because arteries have narrowed or become blocked.

However, any potential cardiovascular benefits must be considered alongside alcohol's association with cancer, liver disease, injuries, and other serious conditions.

When the researchers combined these outcomes, the potential benefits were outweighed by the harmful effects, even among people consuming seven alcoholic drinks per week.

This broader assessment helps explain why a drinking habit that appears beneficial when examining one disease may still increase overall health risks.

Although the findings offer a clearer picture of the long-term dangers of alcohol, the researchers emphasize that the estimates describe risks across populations, not the precise likelihood that any individual will develop a particular disease.

The statistical models relied on "the best possible data," according to the research team. Nevertheless, personal health outcomes can differ considerably depending on genetics, lifestyle, drinking patterns, and other individual factors.

To calculate the overall burden of alcohol consumption, the investigators estimated risks for health conditions already known to have a causal relationship with drinking. They then combined those estimates to assess the total impact.

The researchers also acknowledged that scientific understanding of alcohol's health effects continues to evolve. Emerging evidence suggests that drinking may be associated with additional conditions, including pancreatic cancer, that require further investigation.

"Understanding those relationships, and how much alcohol contributes to those risks, is an area that still needs further work," said Keyes and Shield.

Despite these uncertainties, the results offer an important reference point: alcohol consumption above one drink per day was associated with increased health risks for both men and women.

The researchers believe that giving people more specific information about these risks can help them make better decisions about how much they drink.

"Having a clearer threshold helps people better understand what level of drinking is associated with increased risk and make more informed decisions when drinking."

Why the Findings Matter for U.S. Alcohol Guidelines

The research also raises questions about how scientific evidence is considered when federal drinking recommendations are developed.

In an accompanying editorial, Robert M. Vincent, a former associate administrator for the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, discussed the circumstances surrounding the research and its role in the federal dietary guidance process.

"The Alcohol Intake and Health report was explicitly invited to inform alcohol guidance during development of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030," he writes. "Despite the study's adherence to its mandate, its findings were sidelined."

Vincent's comments highlight concerns about whether the research received appropriate consideration during the development of national recommendations.

The study's findings reinforce the importance of understanding alcohol's cumulative health effects rather than assuming that moderate consumption is beneficial or risk-free. Although individual risks vary, the overall pattern was clear: greater alcohol consumption was associated with greater harm, and the researchers found no overall health advantage to drinking.

The research was funded by Synergy Enterprises Inc. and the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration.

The new rules will also see Rally1 cars use adapted versions of the turbocharged 1.6-liter inline-four engines currently found in the Rally2 class. This means the GR Yaris Rally1 and GR Celica Rally1 will essentially be identical underneath, differentiated only by the bodywork placed atop the chassis.

Changes to the rules mean that WRC teams can now race with cars that do not have a road-going counterpart, although we still expect Toyota to build a new Celica production car. The common chassis and engine in Rally1 next year allowed Toyota to pull up development of the race car, but the road car is still years away and will have little in common with the race car under the skin.

The platform is also expected to usher in a new turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four, codenamed G20E, that could push out north of 400 horsepower.

Even if the Celica doesn’t use this mid-engine platform, it could still be a few years away, since minimal information about the production development has slipped out of Toyota’s walls. #4412. Drinking tea may help protect your heart, but there’s a surprising catch

Drinking tea regularly may offer important benefits for your heart and blood vessels, according to a massive study involving nearly 500,000 adults. Researchers found that people who consumed tea regularly had a lower risk of developing several vascular diseases compared with those who did not drink tea.

However, the findings also revealed some unexpected differences. The type of tea, how strong it was, and even the temperature at which it was consumed were all associated with vascular health. While certain tea drinking habits were linked to a lower risk of disease, drinking tea at extremely high temperatures appeared to have the opposite association.

The research, published in the Journal of Internal Medicine, provides new insights into how an everyday beverage may be connected to long-term cardiovascular health.

Nearly 500,000 Adults Reveal a Link Between Tea and Vascular Health

The study included 485,934 adults in China who were followed for a median of 9.05 years. During that period, researchers recorded 14,863 cases involving several types of vascular disease.

These conditions included cardiovascular disease, which affects the heart and blood vessels, and cerebrovascular disease, which involves blood vessels that supply the brain. The researchers also examined pulmonary heart disease, a condition in which problems involving the lungs or their blood vessels place strain on the heart, and peripheral artery disease, which occurs when arteries carrying blood to areas such as the legs become narrowed or blocked.

Although these conditions affect different parts of the body, they share an important feature: they interfere with the circulation of blood, which delivers oxygen and nutrients to organs and tissues.

When the researchers compared tea drinking habits with the incidence of these diseases, they found that regular tea consumption was associated with an 11% lower risk of the combined vascular outcomes.

The relationship also appeared to vary with the amount consumed. Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk occurred at approximately six to eight cups per day.

This does not necessarily mean that drinking more tea directly prevents disease or that everyone should consume that amount. Because the research was observational, it could identify connections between tea drinking and health outcomes but could not establish that tea itself was responsible for the differences.

Black Tea vs. Green Tea: Does the Type Matter?

One particularly interesting finding involved the type of tea participants consumed.

Black tea showed more consistent associations with a reduced risk of vascular disease than green tea. This suggests that different varieties of tea may not have identical relationships with cardiovascular health.

Both black and green tea come from the same plant, Camellia sinensis, but they undergo different processing methods. Black tea is typically allowed to undergo extensive oxidation, a chemical process that changes the composition of compounds in the leaves, while green tea is processed to limit oxidation.

Tea naturally contains plant compounds known as polyphenols, which have attracted scientific interest because of their antioxidant properties and potential effects on blood vessel function. Antioxidants can help limit certain types of cellular damage caused by reactive molecules.

However, the study does not establish whether these compounds explain the observed differences between black and green tea.

Tea strength also appeared to matter. Participants who drank tea of moderate strength had the lowest associated vascular disease risk, suggesting that stronger tea was not necessarily linked to greater benefits.

Drinking Tea Too Hot May Carry Unexpected Risks

Perhaps the most surprising finding concerned tea temperature.

Although regular tea consumption was generally associated with a reduced risk of vascular disease, drinking tea described as "burning hot" was linked to an increased risk.

The result suggests that the temperature of tea may be an important consideration alongside how much people drink and which variety they prefer.

Very hot beverages can expose tissues in the mouth and digestive tract to high temperatures, but the study did not establish the biological mechanism behind the observed vascular risk. It also did not identify a specific temperature at which tea becomes harmful.

The findings therefore should not be interpreted as proof that drinking extremely hot tea directly causes vascular disease. They do, however, raise questions about whether certain drinking habits could offset some of the favorable associations seen with regular tea consumption.

Tea, Exercise, and Smoking Habits May Work Together

The researchers also examined how tea consumption related to other lifestyle factors, including smoking and physical activity.

Their analysis showed that people who regularly drank tea, were not current smokers, and maintained high levels of physical activity had the lowest vascular disease risk.

"Joint analyses showed that tea consumption, smoking status and physical were collectively associated with vascular risk, with the favorable combination of habitual tea consumption, non-current smoking and high physical activity associated with the lowest risk," the authors wrote.

These results highlight the importance of considering overall lifestyle rather than looking at a single food or beverage in isolation.

Regular physical activity supports cardiovascular health in several ways, including improving circulation, helping regulate blood pressure, and supporting the function of the heart and blood vessels. Avoiding smoking also reduces exposure to substances that can damage blood vessels and increase cardiovascular risk.

Taken together, the findings suggest that tea drinking may be one component of a broader pattern of habits associated with better vascular health.

Although more research is needed to determine whether tea consumption directly influences disease risk, the study offers encouraging evidence that this widely consumed beverage is associated with cardiovascular health. It also highlights an important distinction: when it comes to tea, the amount, variety, strength, and temperature may all be worth considering.

#4411. Best Electric Ride-On Cars for Kids

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

If you’re shopping for a child obsessed with everything automotive, a ride-on electric car makes a great gift. Our staff dads pick their favorites.

This article was updated in November 2026 with new products and information.

For kids with even the slightest interest in cars, trucks, tractors, or fire engines, an electric ride-on is a gift that can transform a childhood. Yes, they can be pricey—but at this point, you might pay gold to have some quiet time in the house. That’s what these ride-on cars can provide: hours of outdoor fun that can help build fine motor skills, gross motor skills, and a real sense of freedom.

From rugged UTVs, dump trucks, realistic sports cars, pickup trucks, fire engines, and even mini motorcycles, there’s an electric ride-on to match every young driver’s interest. We’ve rounded up the best electric ride-on cars for kids that are available today to help you choose the right one.

We’ve even tested some of these with our own families, while others have been rounded up and assessed based on their descriptions and reviews. Either way, here’s a list of the most popular models that feature plenty of neighborhood-cruising fun.

This beautiful Bentley comes in a classy, pearly white. It features working LED headlights, functional scissor doors, a high/low speed switch, and realistic engine noises.

Like all the best electric cars for kids, it also sports a remote control for parents to keep their little racer from driving away. With a top speed of about 3 mph, it offers a full hour of playtime, depending on speed and terrain. Recommended for kids three to six years of age, it has a weight capacity of 66 pounds.

This officially licensed G63 comes with tons of authentic touches, including exhaust pipes, body-detail decals, and opening doors that lock from the outside for safety. The seatbelt and soft-start design prevent kids from being startled by sudden acceleration. The spring suspension ensures smooth rides.

We really like that the side window piece can be removed as kids grow, extending the usable life of the toy.

This is an officially licensed Chevrolet Silverado Trail Boss ride-on pickup truck. It features LED lights, startup sounds, and openable doors, as well as forward/reverse gears and Bluetooth connectivity. The maximum weight capacity is 66 pounds, suitable for ages 37–72 months.

The Peg Perego John Deere Ground Force Tractor is a rugged 12-volt ride-on that brings farm fun to life for kids aged three to seven. With two speeds (2.3 and 4.5 mph), reverse, and automatic brakes, it’s easy for young drivers to operate safely, and parents can use the 4.5-mph lockout for beginners. Farm-style wheels provide traction on grass, dirt, and pavement, and the extra-large stake-side trailer is perfect for hauling toys and treasures around the yard.

For added fun, the tractor features a working FM radio, an adjustable seat, and flip-up armrests for comfort as kids grow. Built to handle plenty of outdoor play, it includes a rechargeable 12-volt battery and charger. Made in the U.S.A., this tractor combines the classic green-and-yellow John Deere style with kid-friendly durability and design for hours of outdoor adventure.

Little adventure seekers will get a kick out of this replica Jeep, with its LED headlights, lockable doors, grid windshield, and off-road tires. It includes a parent remote, a spring suspension, and a safe and manageable max speed of just 2.8 mph. The single-seat version comes in six colors, while the dual-seat version offers seven.

While this ride-on Jeep replica claims to be for kids aged three to six, reviewers say that because of the roll bar it’s actually ideal for younger, smaller kids who can easily slide into the seat. Keep an eye on that weight limit.

This battery-powered ATV delivers rugged fun in a package that looks ready for the trails. Four-wheel suspension helps smooth out bumps, while Bluetooth connectivity, LED lights, and realistic ATV styling add to the excitement. Parents will love that it comes in four color choices, making it easy to match every young rider’s personality. Whether cruising the driveway or exploring the backyard, it’s built for hours of outdoor adventure.

Give your little driver a taste of supercar life with this officially licensed Lamborghini Urus ride-on. Inspired by the luxury SUV’s sleek styling, it features working LED lights, opening doors, spring suspension, realistic engine sounds, and built-in music for an immersive driving experience. Kids can take the wheel themselves or let parents guide the fun with the included remote control. Available in five eye-catching colors, it’s a stylish choice for young car enthusiasts who want to cruise in Lamborghini-inspired fashion.

If you’re wanting to give your kids the ultimate off-road adventurer, look no further than Peg Perego’s Polaris RZR PRO Green Shadow. This 24-volt ride-on features two speeds (that top out at 3.5 and 7.5 mph) as well as reverse, and it comes with enough power and suspension to get over nearly any terrain.

The Green Shadow comes with two seats with a seatbelt, as well as a storage spot in the back for your kids to carry around whatever they need to support their adventures. The rubber wheels are a step up from a lot of the ride-ons on this list and make for a quieter ride when on pavement or asphalt. Other fun features include a built-in radio, working headlights, and a start button.

We’ve been testing one over the past month and our children have loved whipping it around the backyard. Assembly can be tough, but the made-in-Italy construction is solid and should last for years and years to come. Peg Perego recommends this for children between the ages of six and 12, but our four-year-old has no problem tearing up grass in the backyard.

Featuring sirens, speakers, and flashing police lights, this Fire Chief SUV gives children the most realistic experience of driving a fire truck. It’s designed for kids aged three to six, with a maximum weight capacity of 67 pounds.

For chasing pesky bank robbers around the backyard, this ride-on police SUV is a great option. Complete with lights, sirens, a suspension system, and a push-to-talk radio speaker, it’s got just about everything a budding police officer needs.

For little speed demons with big supercar dreams, this officially licensed Lamborghini STO ride-on delivers serious wow factor. The sleek design mirrors the real exotic sports car, while a powerful 24-volt battery, drift mode, and speeds up to 6 mph make every driveway feel like a racetrack. Parents will appreciate the included remote control and safety features, while kids will love the lights, sounds, and realistic driving experience. Recommended for ages three to eight.

Adventurous kids will love this ride-on ATV. LED headlights, a kid-friendly wide seat, and a working horn create a fun and realistic ATV experience. Slow-start technology and enhanced braking make for a safe and comfortable ride. Bluetooth connectivity and a USB port let your kid crank the tunes that drive their adventures.

The Segway GoKart Pro 2 is an adrenaline-fueled go-kart that’s perfect for kids, teens, and adults seeking a high-speed thrill. It can reach speeds up to 26.7 mph and has enough acceleration to make even adults think twice before slamming on the accelerator.

With adjustable frame and steering settings, riders from four-foot-two to six-foot-two can comfortably race, drift, or explore up to 15.5 miles on a single charge. Both my children and I found the GoKart Pro 2 thrilling to ride in the time we spent testing one. The kart’s four riding modes (Eco, Sport, Race, and Manual) make it versatile for both beginner and experienced drivers, with speed caps as low as 5 mph for cautious riding.

My children appreciated the Eco mode’s manageable speed as they got comfortable, while I enjoyed the ability to switch it to Race mode to push its full potential around the neighborhood.

It’s a high-end investment but worth it considering what it offers. For added fun, the Pro 2 also has an engine-sound simulator via an included Bluetooth speaker, which connects to the go-kart to simulate the revs of different engine configurations (V-6, V-8, V-12). This go-kart is thrilling to ride and is sure to offer years of fun for drivers of all skill levels.

This 24-volt tractor is equipped with both a front loader and a detachable trailer. Kids can easily operate the front loader, making scoops, lifts, carries, and dumps from the driver’s seat (which includes a seatbelt). The powerful dual motor (with metal gears) features high and low speeds plus reverse, up to 5 mph. Max weight limit is 65 pounds.

For older kids, a little electric motorcycle might be the move. Razor makes the excellent Dirt Rocket in many variations, but the one shown here (the MX125) is geared more toward the seven-to-eight-year-old range. Though if something more exciting is of interest, Razor scales this model up in power (and age suggestion).

All feature dual suspension and riser handlebars, pneumatic knobby tires, a retractable kickstand, and hand-operated brakes. While all are undeniably cute and cool, these motocross bikes are not toys for small children.

Little land movers will feel right at home in this ride-on dump truck. It’s the ultimate fun machine. With two 35-watt motors, it features two speeds when manually controlled by the child using the foot pedal, and three speeds (top speed 3 mph) with the parent remote control. It also has a built-in Bluetooth speaker and a working dump bed. With automatic lifting and an extra shovel, kids can pitch in with the yardwork by carrying leaf piles and debris.

Little bikers will love this chopper-style “motorcycle” (that’s really a trike, so it won’t fall over). It features a working, adjustable LED headlight, pedal operation, forward/reverse, and more. The only things missing are a black t-shirt and a goatee. Designed for kids three years and up, with a weight limit of 66 pounds.

If your kid is ready to take to the not-so-open road, here’s what to look for in an electric car for kids.

While it can be tempting to get a ride-on that your child will grow into and use for years, there are safety risks involved with choosing one that’s too large or powerful for your kid to control easily.

Most electric ride-on cars feature speeds between 1.5 and 5 mph, but the more powerful you go, the higher that top speed climbs. Check the manufacturer’s recommendations for age and weight. Some even offer parental remote controls and seatbelts, while others let you remove features such as side panels as your child grows.

The biggest concern safety-wise with these toys is not so much the product itself but where the children take them. Hilly terrain can cause them to flip, and bodies of water aren’t meant to be driven through. It’s also very important to convey that these aren’t meant to be taken near a road, as their small profile can be difficult to see by drivers of normal-size vehicles.

Electric ride-ons come in multiple styles to match kids’ varying interests. Classic cars and trucks mimic real-life vehicles, offering features such as working headlights and sound effects for a realistic experience. ATVs and UTVs are built for rougher terrain with “all-terrain” tires and higher clearances. For kids who love motorcycles, bike-style ride-ons can often include training wheels for added stability.

Most electric ride-ons are powered by rechargeable batteries, typically ranging from six to 24 volts. Higher voltage generally translates to more power and a longer run time, but it’s important to match the power to the terrain and age level.

Models with 12-volt batteries provide a good balance of speed and battery life for mixed-terrain use, while 24-volt versions can handle tougher trails and inclines. Be mindful that all batteries will gradually lose capacity, so check for compatible replacement options if you plan to use the ride-on for years to come.

Interactive features can make a big difference in the overall experience. Some ride-ons include Bluetooth speakers or FM radios, letting kids listen to their favorite songs while driving. Others offer realistic details such as functional doors, working headlights and taillights, and engine sound effects.

#4410. Fat Fender Garage’s GT/FX Pairs Sporty Looks with an 800-HP V-8

This radical truck is based on a 1956 Ford F-100 but swaps in a new chassis, an 800-hp Coyote V-8, and a modernized cabin with leather bucket seats.

Ford has produced a diverse array of vehicles in its 123-year history, from workhorses like the bestselling F-series trucks to supercars like the GT supercar. Now, a small outfit seeks to blend the philosophies of those two vehicles. Fat Fender Garage, a restoration shop based in Arizona, has revealed the GT/FX at SEMA, taking the body of a 1956 F-100 truck and giving it performance chops meant to emulate the capabilities of the Ford GT.

The GT/FX’s steel body was drastically reshaped by Fat Fender Garage, with a flatter hood and roof and wider front and rear fenders giving it a more aggressive stance. The custom running boards blend neatly into the rear fenders, while a chin splitter up front and a rear diffuser swiped from a Mustang GT350 give the GT/FX a track-ready look.

See all results for used Ford for sale near 95051

The bed now features distinctive flared edges, and the tailgate drops down with the push of a button. The side-view mirrors are fashioned from carbon fiber, and the gray paint job is completed with a black racing stripe just offset to the left. The only thing left untouched was the grille, maintaining a tie-back to the original F-100.

Behind that grille sits a Gen 3 Ford Coyote 5.0-liter V-8 with a 3.0-liter Whipple supercharger strapped on top, pushing out 800 horsepower and 750 pound-feet of torque. The hearty engine is paired with Ford’s 10R80 10-speed automatic transmission, which routes that muscle to HRE wheels wearing Toyo Proxes Sport 2 tires, measuring a beefy 315/35R-20 at the rear. Stopping duties are handled by Wilwood disc brakes with six-piston front calipers and four-piston rear calipers.

The cabin features modern-looking bucket seats; a modern screen and buttons are also part of the transformation, but they’re discreetly integrated. Plus, there’s a concealed climate-control system that blows air through a hidden vent, and there’s also interior LED lighting and a modern audio system.

The GT/FX showcases the breadth of Fat Fender Garage’s abilities, from paint to interior trim and exhaust setups. The truck even rides on the company’s own FF1 Performance Coilover chassis, which is designed to provide sporty handling despite the vintage truck’s body on top. Between the bodywork, the cabin, the powertrain, and the chassis, Fat Fender Garage went all in on transforming the F-100 from a utilitarian hauler into a sport truck that blends classic styling with modern power.

Prepare to say goodbye to Range Rover’s two most affordable models, as the Evoque and Velar celebrate their final model year in production. The company has confirmed to British outlet Autocar that the volume sellers will cease production after 2027 and be replaced by the new Range Rover GT.

“Both Range Rover Velar and Range Rover Evoque will continue to be sold in selected global markets where demand remains strong, throughout 2027,” a JLR spokesperson told Car and Driver. “Production of both models will end in mid-2027 in line with their natural product lifecycles, as JLR’s manufacturing facilities transition to build its next generation of vehicles.”

The Evoque and Velar’s sales have accounted for just 6000 of Land Rover’s U.S. sales through this year. The two SUVs are attractive not only for their styling but also for their relatively low prices compared with the six-figure ask for the flagship Range Rover SUV. Like the Jaguar Type 01, the Range Rover GT takes the shape of a long and low sedan-like vehicle with a minimalist interior and an all-wheel-drive electric powertrain. The Range Rover GT will launch first as an EV, but the company says the platform is capable of hosting gas and hybrid powertrains as well. It stands to reason that a Discovery Sport model could be revived in the future, possibly as an EV, to serve as an entry point to the Discovery lineup.

#4408. Scientists discover surprising heart benefits of eating avocado and mango every day

Eating mango and avocado every day could offer unexpected benefits for heart health, according to new research. In a study lasting just eight weeks, adults with prediabetes who regularly ate both fruits experienced improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure, without gaining weight or consuming more calories.

The findings could be especially relevant to the one in three (98 million) Americans with prediabetes, a condition in which blood sugar levels are elevated but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, the research suggests that incorporating these two nutrient-rich fruits into everyday meals may help support cardiovascular health.

Researchers at Illinois Institute of Technology (Illinois Tech) investigated the effects of an Avocado-Mango (AM) diet that included one medium Hass avocado and one cup of fresh mango each day. Participants followed this eating plan for eight weeks, while a comparison group consumed a similar diet in which the fruits were replaced with carbohydrate-based foods containing equivalent calories.

The results revealed notable differences between the groups, particularly in how well their blood vessels functioned and how their blood pressure changed over time.

One of the clearest improvements involved the ability of blood vessels to expand as blood flows through them. This flexibility helps maintain healthy circulation and is an important indicator of cardiovascular health.

To evaluate this response, researchers measured flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a commonly used test of endothelial function (blood vessel health). The endothelium is the thin layer of cells lining the inside of blood vessels, where it helps regulate circulation and the widening and narrowing of arteries.

Among participants eating avocado and mango, the measurement increased significantly to 6.7%. In contrast, it declined to 4.6% in the control group. The difference suggests that regularly consuming these fruits may help blood vessels function more effectively.

Blood pressure measurements also showed encouraging changes, especially among male participants. Men in the control group experienced an average increase of 5 points (mmHg) in central blood pressure, while those consuming avocado and mango saw a reduction of approximately 1.9 points.

Diastolic blood pressure, the lower number in a blood pressure reading, reflects the pressure inside arteries when the heart relaxes between beats. Maintaining healthy levels is important because elevated blood pressure can place additional strain on the cardiovascular system. Researchers noted that the differences observed in the study could be clinically meaningful if they persist over time.

Importantly, the cardiovascular improvements occurred without significant changes in participants' body weight or total calorie consumption. This suggests that the nutritional quality of the foods people eat may influence heart health even when their weight remains stable.

“This research reinforces the power of food-first strategies to help reduce cardiovascular disease risk, particularly in vulnerable populations like those with prediabetes,” said Britt Burton-Freeman, PhD, Principal Investigator and Professor at Illinois Tech. “It’s an encouraging message: small, nutrient-dense additions—like incorporating avocado and mango into meals and snacks—may support heart health without the need for strict rules or major dietary overhauls.”

Beyond the improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure, participants eating mango and avocado consumed more fiber, vitamin C, and monounsaturated fat. These nutrients are associated with cardiovascular wellness and may help explain some of the observed benefits.

Researchers also identified improvements in certain indicators of kidney health, including estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), a measurement used to assess how effectively the kidneys filter waste from the blood.

However, the fruits did not produce significant improvements in every health measurement. Cholesterol levels, blood sugar, and markers of inflammation remained largely unchanged compared with the control group.

Together, the results suggest that regularly including nutrient-rich fruits in the diet could be a practical way to support cardiovascular health, particularly for people with prediabetes who face an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

Although mango and avocado have very different flavors and nutritional profiles, they provide complementary nutrients that support several aspects of cardiovascular and metabolic health.

Mango provides dietary fiber (2g/serving, 7% DV, Mango serving size: ¾ cup) and is an excellent source of vitamin C (50% DV). Vitamin C is an antioxidant that helps protect cells from damage, while fiber contributes to healthy digestion and may help with blood sugar regulation, weight management, and cardiovascular wellness.

Avocado offers another combination of potentially beneficial nutrients. It contains fiber (3g/serving, 11% DV, Avocado serving size: 50 g (1/3 of a medium avocado)), which plays a role in managing cholesterol, blood sugar, and body weight.

It also supplies unsaturated fats (6g unsaturated fats), which can support heart health by helping reduce LDL cholesterol, often called bad cholesterol, when they replace less healthy fats in the diet. Additionally, avocado contains potassium (250mg, 6% DV), a mineral involved in regulating blood pressure.

By providing fiber, antioxidants, healthy fats, and potassium, mango and avocado offer a convenient way to increase the nutritional value of everyday meals. However, the study did not establish whether eating the two fruits together provides greater benefits than consuming either fruit separately.

Incorporating these fruits into meals does not require a complicated eating plan. Their contrasting flavors and textures make them useful ingredients in salads, smoothies, and grain bowls.

For example, fresh mango can add sweetness to a savory dish, while avocado contributes a rich, creamy texture. Both can be used in recipes such as Mango Avocado Tuna Ceviche or an Avocado and Mango Topper.

Additional recipes and nutritional information are available at Mango.org and LoveOneToday.com.

The investigation included 82 adults between the ages of 25 and 60 who had prediabetes and were classified as having overweight or obesity (BMI 25–35 kg/m2). All participants were generally healthy, did not smoke, were not following specialized diets, and had no major chronic medical conditions.

Over eight weeks, participants followed calorie-controlled eating plans modeled on typical American dietary patterns. One group ate a medium Hass avocado and a cup of fresh mango daily, while the control group received carbohydrate-based alternatives with comparable calorie content.

To make the comparison as consistent as possible, researchers prepared and supplied meals covering 75% of each participant's estimated daily calorie needs. Participants chose their remaining foods independently, allowing some flexibility while helping the researchers limit differences between the two diets and encourage adherence.

The primary measurement was flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a noninvasive method for assessing how effectively blood vessels respond to increased circulation. Researchers also examined blood pressure, blood sugar, and other metabolic indicators, inflammation, kidney function, and dietary nutrient intake.

Despite the additional fruits, the avocado and mango group did not experience significant changes in body weight or overall calorie intake. This finding suggests that incorporating nutrient-dense foods into an otherwise balanced diet may improve certain aspects of cardiometabolic health without necessarily contributing to weight gain.

The study had several strengths, including its carefully controlled feeding approach, two parallel comparison groups, and emphasis on whole fruits rather than isolated nutrients or supplements.

However, researchers also acknowledged important limitations. The intervention lasted only eight weeks, so it remains unclear whether the improvements would persist over months or years. The participants also represented a relatively narrow population of adults with prediabetes and overweight or obesity, meaning the findings may not apply equally to people with different health conditions or dietary habits.

The research measured cardiovascular risk indicators rather than long-term outcomes such as heart attacks or strokes. Larger and longer studies will be needed to determine whether the observed changes translate into lasting reductions in cardiovascular disease risk.

Nevertheless, the findings offer an encouraging indication that relatively modest changes in food choices may benefit blood vessel health, even without weight loss or a major dietary overhaul.

This study was supported through an unrestricted grant from the National Mango Board (NMB) and the Hass Avocado Board (HAB). NMB and HAB had no role in the study design or findings.

#4407. Gentle Mates GC come from a map down to beat Shopify Rebellion Gold and reach Game Changers final

Gentle Mates GC, on their Championship debut, beat Shopify Rebellion Gold 2-1 in the upper bracket final in São Paulo. The French-based side go into Sunday's best-of-five grand final with a two-map ban advantage, while Shopify Rebellion Gold must come through the lower final.

Gentle Mates GC are into the grand final of the VCT Game Changers Championship 2026. They beat Shopify Rebellion Gold 2-1 in the upper bracket final in São Paulo on Friday 30 October. The French-based side dropped the opening map and then took the next two. Both teams had arrived at the match with every map at the event won.

Shopify Rebellion Gold won map one, which lasted 53 minutes. On the second map they fought back to 10-10, but Gentle Mates closed it out 13-11 after 55 minutes. The decider on Summit ran for 57 minutes and finished 13-10 to Gentle Mates.

Coming through the upper bracket gives Gentle Mates a two-map ban advantage in the grand final. Shopify Rebellion Gold, led at the event by interim in-game leader alexis, drop into the lower bracket final against KRÜ Blaze.

This is Gentle Mates’ first appearance at the Championship. Their line-up of Marti, Nami, Wens, tokameite and berryx reached the upper final with 2-0 wins over Team Liquid Brazil and MIBR GC. Their last three EMEA Stage 3 results before the event were wins over G2 Gozen and SK Nebula, both 2-1, and a 3-2 defeat to G2 Gozen.

The Elo power rankings already had Gentle Mates ahead. They sit fourth with a rating of 1844 and a 33-7 record from 40 rated matches. Shopify Rebellion Gold are sixth on 1809, with a 40-20 record from 60 rated matches.

Shopify Rebellion Gold had cleared SK Nebula and KRÜ Blaze without losing a map. Before travelling, they beat FlyQuest RED 3-1 and 2-1 and SwimTrek Blue 2-0 in North America Stage 2. At last year’s Championship in Seoul, Team Liquid Brazil beat them 3-2 in the title match.

The lower bracket final is a rematch. Shopify Rebellion Gold beat KRÜ Blaze in the upper semi-final.
